l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JUNE, JULY & AUGUST 1661 June 1st.
s: From June 1 to June 5, the diarist and Sir W. Pen inspect ships at Woolwich and Deptford and conduct business connected with an impending voyage. The diarist discusses Wardrobe responsibilities with my Lord, who expresses confidence in him and promises him first refusal of Mr. Young’s place for his father if it becomes vacant. The diarist and Mr. Creed obtain financial imprests and seek ammunition for my Lord’s ships, while the Navy Office conducts its regular business. The diarist also spends time with family and colleagues, attends church and the theatre, and takes part in social and musical activities.

l: Sir W. Pen, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JUNE, JULY & AUGUST 1661 June 1st.
s: Sir W. Pen accompanied the diarist by water to Woolwich and Deptford on June 1 to inspect ships and give orders concerning their readiness to go forth. He later attended the Navy Office, went bowling with Sir R. Slingsby, and returned home with the diarist.

l: Lord Sandwich, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JUNE, JULY & AUGUST 1661 June 1st.
s: My Lord instructed the diarist about Wardrobe business during his absence and said that he intended to join the diarist and Mr. Moore in managing it if Mr. Townsend died. He expressed great confidence in the diarist and promised to give him the refusal of Mr. Young’s place in the Wardrobe if it became vacant. The diarist also obtained my Lord’s imprest of L1000 and sought ammunition for his ships.

l: Mr. Creed, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JUNE, JULY & AUGUST 1661 June 1st.
s: Mr. Creed’s imprest of L10,000 was signed against the voyage. He dined with the diarist, accompanied him to the Tower to seek ammunition for my Lord’s ships, and walked with him around the Tower.

l: the Wardrobe, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JUNE, JULY & AUGUST 1661 June 1st.
s: The Wardrobe was the subject of my Lord’s instructions to the diarist concerning its management during his absence. My Lord proposed joining the diarist and Mr. Moore in its business if Mr. Townsend died, and promised the diarist first refusal of Mr. Young’s place for his father if it became vacant.

l: the Navy Office, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JUNE, JULY & AUGUST 1661 June 1st.
s: The diarist attended the Navy Office on several days to conduct and sit over official business. The office was also involved in arrangements concerning nearby lodgings, though the houses considered by the Comptroller and the diarist did not suit them.

l: the voyage, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JUNE, JULY & AUGUST 1661 June 1st.
s: Imprests for my Lord and Mr. Creed were signed against the voyage. The diarist and others inspected ships and made preparations for their going forth.

l: ships, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JUNE, JULY & AUGUST 1661 June 1st.
s: On June 1, the diarist, Sir W. Pen, and Mr. Gauden went from ship to ship at Woolwich and Deptford to give orders and assess their readiness to go forth. The diarist and Mr. Creed later sought ammunition at the Tower for my Lord’s ships.

l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The diarist spends these days visiting Greenwich, Whitehall, the Wardrobe, the office, and the Theatre, while dining and drinking with various acquaintances. Lieutenant Lambert, now Captain of the Norwich, explains ships to him during a water journey to Greenwich. The diarist learns from my Lord that Mr. Townsend is to reveal the whole mystery of the Wardrobe and that he may become Townsend's deputy. He sees Bartholomew Faire at the Theatre, visits the Wardrobe with his wife, and discusses ecclesiastical matters with Dean Fuller.

l: Lieutenant Lambert, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: Lieutenant Lambert has been made Captain of the Norwich. He takes the diarist by water to Greenwich, explains various matters concerning ships, and later accompanies him to Mr. Holland's house.

l: Whitehall, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The diarist goes to Whitehall several times, seeking my Lord and later meeting Dean Fuller there. He also returns to Whitehall after visiting Mr. Pierce and drinks with Mr. Symons at the Swan tavern.

l: Lord Sandwich, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: My Lord tells the diarist to go to Mr. Townsend, who is to disclose the whole mystery of the Wardrobe to him. He also says that the diarist will be made deputy to Mr. Townsend in case Townsend dies during my Lord's absence.

l: the Wardrobe, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The diarist visits the Wardrobe, where he dines with my Lady and is kindly treated. He later brings his wife there to dine, and she is received with considerable attention.

l: Mr. Townsend, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: Mr. Townsend has been ordered by my Lord to reveal the whole mystery of the Wardrobe to the diarist and no one else. The diarist is to become his deputy because of the possibility of Townsend's death during my Lord's absence.

l: the Wardrobe business, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The diarist is promised an important role in the Wardrobe administration: my Lord intends to make him deputy to Mr. Townsend. Townsend is to explain the administration's whole mystery to him.

l: the Theatre, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The diarist goes to the Theatre with Mr. Shepley and Mr. Creed and sees Bartholomew Faire. He considers the play admirable and well acted, though excessively profane and abusive.

l: Bartholomew Faire, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: Bartholomew Faire is performed at the Theatre for the first time in the present day. The diarist finds it most admirable and well acted, but too profane and abusive.

l: the narrator's wife, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The diarist's wife wears a black silk gown laced all over with black gimp lace and looks very pretty in it. She walks with him to the Wardrobe, dines there, and remains with my Lady after the diarist leaves.

l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The narrator's lord is to go to Algier to settle business, put the fleet in order, and return to Lisbone with three ships to meet the following fleet. He entrusts the narrator with overseeing the great preparation during his absence under orders from my Lord Chancellor and Edward Montagu. The office agrees to write to the Duke of York about its severe shortage of money and inability to obtain supplies without personal security. The office's credit has fallen so low that suppliers will no longer sell to it without such security.

l: fleet, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The fleet is to be put in order at Algier. The narrator's lord is to return to Lisbone with three ships and meet the fleet that is to follow him.

l: my Lord Chancellor, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: My Lord Chancellor is to give the narrator orders concerning the great preparation during the narrator's lord's absence.

l: Edward Montagu, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: Edward Montagu is to give the narrator orders concerning the great preparation during the narrator's lord's absence.

l: Lord Sandwich, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The narrator's lord is to go to Algier to settle business and put the fleet in order there, then return to Lisbone with three ships. He entrusts the narrator with overseeing the great preparation during his absence.

l: great preparation, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The great preparation is to be overseen by the narrator during the narrator's lord's absence, under orders from my Lord Chancellor and Edward Montagu.

l: the Navy Office, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The office agrees to write to the Duke of York about its sad condition and lack of money. Its men are unable to serve it further without money.

l: Sir George Carteret, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: Sir G. Carteret attends the office and joins in agreeing on a letter to the Duke of York about the office's financial difficulties.

l: Duke of York, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The office is to receive a letter informing him of its lack of money, its inability to obtain further supplies, and the low state of its credit.

l: money, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The office lacks money, and its men are not able to serve it more without some money.

l: the office's credit, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The office's credit has fallen so low that no one will sell it anything without personal security from those involved.

l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The narrator spends time with Captain Rolt, Ferrers, and others before arranging a cloth purchase for my Lord and obtaining an advance through Alderman Backwell. On the 13th, the narrator accompanies my Lord from Whitehall to Deptford and boards the Dutch yacht with him. My Lord becomes angry when W. Howe delays bringing his things, but they eventually sail, and the narrator takes leave of my Lord with expressions of respect and a five-gun salute. The narrator then returns toward London by boat with Captain Ferrers.

l: Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The narrator visits Lambeth, works at home, and writes a letter to the Duke. He arranges for £300 of cloth to be purchased for my Lord through Alderman Backwell, accompanies my Lord to Deptford, and takes leave of him aboard the Dutch yacht before returning toward London with Captain Ferrers.

l: Lord Sandwich, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: My Lord requires £300 worth of cloth to give as presents among the Turks in Barbary. He travels from Whitehall to Deptford, boards the Dutch yacht, becomes angry when W. Howe is late with his things, and then sails after taking leave of the King and his friends.

l: the cloth, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The cloth is intended for presents to the Turks in Barbary. Mr. Shaw offers the narrator £300 for my Lord to purchase it with, and my Lord orders Mr. Creed to advance that amount through Alderman Backwell.

l: Dutch yacht, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The Dutch yacht is boarded by my Lord and the narrator at Deptford. It waits while W. Howe brings my Lord's things, then sails from Erith after dinner.

l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The diarist manages the purchase and shipment of cloth for my Lord, arranging scarlet, purple, and black cloth and linen, and eventually sending it by a Margate Hoy after other plans fail. He recovers from a painful cold and spends several days overseeing painters who finish work on his stairs. He visits friends and relatives, including my father, my Lady, Captain Lambert's household, and Jack Cole, and attends to office and financial business. By the end of the unit, he is pleased with the completed stairs and relieved of his illness and household troubles.

l: Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The diarist arranges the purchase and delivery of cloth for my Lord, attends to office, household, and financial matters, and visits family and friends. He recovers from his illness, supervises the painters' work on his stairs, and is pleased when it is completed.

l: the diarist's father, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: My father advises and assists with the cloth business. He visits the diarist, drinks his morning draft with him, discusses the cloth, and helps resolve on two pieces each of scarlet, purple, and black, with £50 in linen.

l: Lord Sandwich, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: My Lord is the intended recipient of the cloth. The diarist writes to him to report what has been arranged.

l: the painters, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The painters work on the diarist's stairs. Their progress causes the diarist some vexation because of delays, but they finish the work by the 20th, to his great content.

l: a Margate Hoy, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: A Margate Hoy is hired to carry the cloth and related goods. The diarist sends the things aboard it late at night, hoping they will reach the Downs by the following night.

l: the cloth, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The cloth is being bought for my Lord and consists of two pieces of scarlet, two of purple, and two of black, together with £50 in linen. The diarist struggles to find a reliable way to send it.

l: garden stairs, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The stairs are being painted by the diarist's workmen. The work is finished by the 20th and pleases the diarist greatly.

l: the cloth shipment, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The cloth shipment is delayed when the purser of the King's yacht does not come for it and the diarist learns that the Duke of York has already departed. After considering sending it by carrier or by a vessel hired for the purpose, he sends it by a Margate Hoy.

l: the diarist's illness, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The diarist's illness is a painful cold caused by playing in the water. He stays home, keeps warm, breaks wind, and gains relief; by the 19th he reports that he is very well again.

l: the painters' work, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The painters' work on the stairs is delayed and troubles the diarist for much of the 18th and 19th. It is completed on the 20th, leaving him greatly content.

l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The narrator met uncle Wight at the Exchequer and went home with him to dinner. At dinner, the narrator and Mr. Norbury discussed Mr. Norbury's wife's house and land at Brampton, which the narrator found too much to buy. The narrator later went to the office and was pleased to see the house beginning to be clean. On the 22nd, the narrator dined with Lord Crew and was very much made of by Lord Crew and his lady.

l: uncle Wight, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The narrator met uncle Wight at the Exchequer and went home with him to dinner.

l: Mr. Norbury, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: Mr. Norbury discussed his wife's house and land at Brampton with the narrator over dinner.

l: Mr. Norbury's house and land at Brampton, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The narrator learned about Mr. Norbury's wife's house and land at Brampton and found it too much to buy.

l: Lord Crew, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The narrator dined with Lord Crew on the 22nd and was very much made of by Lord Crew and his lady.

l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: Pepys spent time with Luellin and Blirton, attended church, socialized with Sir W. Batten and others, and visited Islington. He was pleased that his house had become very clean and neat, and his father came to see it on Midsummer-day. Elizabeth Pepys was unwell, with a sore belly that she believed had become dangerous. At Graye’s Inn Walks, Pepys considered Mrs. Frances Butler the greatest beauty he had ever seen.

l: the narrator's house, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: Pepys found his house very clean and was greatly pleased with it. On Midsummer-day, his father came to see it after it was finished and found it very neat.

l: the narrator's wife, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: Elizabeth Pepys was not well, so Pepys went with Sir W. Batten to dinner instead of remaining at home. Dr. Williams came to see her, as her sore belly had grown dangerous in her opinion.

l: Sir W. Batten, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: Sir W. Batten accompanied Pepys home to dinner and later spent time with him at his own house. He was among the company who went to church after dinner.

l: Mrs. Frances Butler, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: Pepys saw Mrs. Frances Butler at Graye’s Inn Walks and described her as the greatest beauty he had ever seen. She was identified as Monsieur L'Impertinent’s sister.

l: Pepys's wife's illness, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: Pepys’s wife was unwell, and her sore belly was described as having become dangerous as she thought. Dr. Williams came to see her.

l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The diarist begins singing lessons with Mr. Mage and spends time with family and visitors. He learns from a letter from his aunt that Robert has become ill with dizziness, prompting his father to travel to attend to Robert's business. The diarist discusses with his father how to present a proposed land purchase to Robert, offering £600 immediately and £150 annually for land yielding £50 per year. He later attends a performance of "Bartholomew Fayre" with Lady Batten, Mrs. Rebecca Allen, Mrs. Thompson, and others.

l: the diarist's father, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The diarist's father learns from the letter from the diarist's aunt that Robert is seriously unwell and needs help with his business. He plans to travel to Robert, and the diarist advises him on how to discuss the proposed land purchase.

l: Sir W. Batten, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: Sir William Batten sits with the diarist and others until late, and the diarist provides a substantial collation. Later, the diarist stays late at Sir William Batten's house after attending "Bartholomew Fayre."

l: the letter from the diarist's aunt, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The letter informs the diarist's father that Robert has been taken with dizziness in his head and that his help is wanted with Robert's business. The letter leads the diarist's father to plan a journey to Robert.

l: Aunt Fenner, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The diarist's aunt writes to the diarist's father that Robert is seriously unwell and requires his assistance.

l: uncle Robert, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: Robert is suffering from dizziness in his head, and his condition is considered serious. His business requires the diarist's father's attention, and the diarist wants his father to discuss buying land with him.

l: land, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The diarist is considering buying land that would yield £50 per year. He proposes paying £600 immediately and £150 annually for the remainder.

l: the land-purchase plan, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The diarist plans to have his father present the purchase as an offer of £600 in ready money followed by £150 per year until the price is complete. He wants Robert to think he is a greater saver than he really is, since he has no more than £500 in ready money.

l: Bartholomew Faire, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: "Bartholomew Fayre" is performed very well, and the diarist attends the performance with Lady Batten, Mrs. Rebecca Allen, Mrs. Thompson, and others in two coaches.

l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The writer spent the 28th practising singing, visiting his Lady, working at the office, and going with Sir W. Pen to Moorefields to watch wrestling. On the 29th, the writer and both Sir Williams examined delays in preparing ships at Deptford, then met Mr. Chetwind, Gregory, Hartlibb, and Mr. Kipps at the Bell at the Maypole in the Strand. Mr. Chetwind, formerly consumptive, had become very fat and sallow from chewing tobacco and praised Hooker's Ecclesiastical Polity as the book that made him a Christian. On the 30th, the writer observed that the trade of briefs had become so constant that he and others resolved to give no more to them.

l: Sir W. Pen, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: Sir W. Pen accompanied the writer in his coach to Moorefields, where they walked and watched wrestling between north and west countrymen.

l: our old club, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: Several members of the writer's old club, including Mr. Chetwind, Gregory, and Hartlibb, met with the writer at the Bell at the Maypole in the Strand and talked and drank with much pleasure.

l: Mr. Chetwind, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: Mr. Chetwind had become very fat and sallow from chewing tobacco, whereas he had previously been consumptive. He commended Hooker's Ecclesiastical Polity as the best book and the only one that had made him a Christian.

l: the Bell at the Maypole in the Strand, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The Bell at the Maypole in the Strand was the place where the writer met Mr. Chetwind, Gregory, Hartlibb, and Mr. Kipps for drinking and conversation.

l: Hooker's Ecclesiastical Polity, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: Hooker's Ecclesiastical Polity was praised by Mr. Chetwind as the best book and the only one that had made him a Christian. The writer decided to buy it shortly.

l: trade of briefs, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The trade of briefs had become a constant practice every Sunday. The writer and others resolved to give no more to it.

l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The speaker attended a sermon, had dinner with his wife, and went to Whitehall with Sir Williams to report to the Duke of York about why the ships had not been sent out. The ships could not leave the river because the wind was against them. The speaker later walked alone in Graye's Inn Walk, returned home tired, and found his wife out of order but not sick. The Portuguese Embassador came to White Hall to take leave of the King before ending matters with the Queen and sending her over.

l: Duke of York, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The Duke of York met the speaker and Sir Williams at Whitehall to receive an account of where the fault lay in the failure to send out the ships.

l: Whitehall, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The speaker went to Whitehall with Sir Williams and met the Duke of York there. The Portuguese Embassador also came to White Hall to take leave of the King.

l: Portuguese Embassador, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The Portuguese Embassador came to White Hall to take leave of the King.

l: Queen, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The Portuguese Embassador was going to end all with the Queen and send her over. The speaker hoped to make up his expenses by helping prepare things to send with the next fleet to the Queen.

l: order to report on the ships, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: An order had been sent to the speaker and Sir Williams the previous day to give the Duke of York an account of where the fault lay in the ships not being sent out.

l: ships, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The ships could not get out of the river because the wind had been against them.

l: failure to send out the ships, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The failure to send out the ships was attributed solely to the wind being against them, which prevented them from leaving the river.

l: Portuguese ambassador's departure and arrangements for the Queen, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The Portuguese Embassador came to take leave of the King and was going to end all with the Queen and send her over.

l: fleet, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
s: The speaker hoped to recover his recent expenses during the summer by helping get things ready to send with the next fleet to the Queen.

l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JULY 1661 July 1st.
s: The diarist bought household goods, including a chest of drawers and an Indian gown, attended to office and domestic affairs, and continued singing lessons with Theodore Goodgroome. He visited Sir William Davenant's Opera, where the second part of "The Siege of Rhodes" was performed for the King and the Queen of Bohemia, though the Eunuch was hissed off the stage. He also learned of the serious illness of his uncle and the death of Mr. Saml. Crew from spotted fever. On July 4th, he saw "Claracilla" at the Theatre and noted that the house was unusually empty because of the Opera.
